govt_bonds.rationale: Headwinds and tailwinds roughly offset. Against duration: October payrolls beat (+165k vs ~59k expected, AHE +0.4% m/m), ISM manufacturing prices paid stayed above 70 (75.2), CME pricing for a December Fed hike was ~77% after the report, and the BoE hiked to 4% on 5 Nov with members signalling more. In favour: Brent fell ~13% on the week on US-Iran de-escalation hopes, the Democratic midterm sweep was read by JPMorgan and BondBloxx as reducing deficit growth, Treasury held coupon sizes ($125bn refunding), and haven demand during the AI equity rout pulled the 2-year down roughly 10-13bp on the week (to ~4.5%) while the 10-year held near 4.86% and the 30-year near 5.27%. Note Treasury dropped 'at least' from its coupon-size guidance, which strategists read as a hint of larger auctions in 2027-28.

The AI equity rout and talk of data-centre restrictions after the midterms hit the issuers driving that supply, while the macro backdrop of global rate hikes raises refinancing costs. Spreads are still tight in absolute terms (ICE BofA US HY OAS 3.48% on 5 Nov per FRED, up from 3.32% on 4 Nov) and demand for quality deals held (Apple $7.5bn), so a mild rather than strong headwind.

regime_notes: Risk-off this week. The defining macro theme is a global tightening cycle in response to the Middle East energy shock: the Fed held at 3.75-4.00% on 28 Oct with two hawkish dissents and markets price ~75-77% odds of a December hike after the October payroll beat (+165k, wages +0.4% m/m); the BoE hiked 8-1 to 4% on 5 Nov and projects CPI near 5% by mid-2027; the RBA reportedly hiked to 4.85% on 3 Nov (secondary sources only); the ECB (2.50%) and BoJ (1.25%) held at end-October but flagged December hikes. On top of that, the Democratic midterm sweep triggered an AI-led global equity rout (S&P 500 -4.4% on 5 Nov, VIX ~25.6), with havens bid. Partial offsets: Brent fell about 13% on the week on US-Iran de-escalation hopes, which lowers the inflation impulse, and divided government is read as fiscally restraining, which helps the long end. US activity data are strong (ISM manufacturing 55.5), so this is a rates-and-valuation risk-off, not a recession scare.
